docs.text: tuvl ¶ Typed workflows of agents — deterministic where they can be, bounded where they can't — on a durable, journaled runtime, built spec-first. tuvl 2.0.0 — released 20 October 2026, public beta now tuvl 2.0 is a redesign with no 1.x compatibility layer: workflows are graphs of typed agents , every run is durable and journaled, and projects are built from specs. See what's new . Until the release, install the public beta 2.0.0b3 — see Installation . Versions follow SemVer . Try it live — no install Run any example in a throwaway browser sandbox at try.tuvl.online with the Insight editor. Pronounced "Thoo-val" (തൂവൽ) in Malayalam — a feather. What is tuvl? ¶ A tuvl workflow is a graph of agents . Each agent has a typed contract — inputs , outputs , the signals it emits — and an engine that implements it. Signals route to the next agent or a named end. tuvl checks the whole graph statically (contracts, data flow, types, policy, worst-case cost) and runs it on a durable runtime that records everything it does. kind: Workflow version: tuvl/v2 metadata: { name: refund_flow, description: Handle a refund request } spec: models: [Order, Refund] trigger: http: { path: /api/refunds, method: POST } input: { order_id: uuid, reason: str } agents: - id: load_order description: Load the order engine: tool inputs: { order_id: uuid } outputs: { order: Order } tool: { use: db, model: Order, op: read, where: { id: "{{ order_id }}" } } routes: { default: triage, not_found: END.missing, error: END.failed } - id: triage description: Decide how the refund is handled engine: decide inputs: { order: Order, reason: str } outputs: { lane: "enum[auto, review]" } decide: rules: - { when: "order.total > 500", then: review } - { when: "true", then: auto } routes: { auto: issue_refund, review: approval, error: END.failed } # issue_refund (code) and approval (human) … outputs: default: { status: 200, body: { refund_id: "{{ refund.id }}" } } missing: { status: 404, body: { error: unknown order } } failed: { status: 500, rollback: true, body: { error: refund failed } } Key features ¶ Seven engines, one contract code , tool (DB/HTTP/MCP), decide (rules, then a model), llm , loop (bounded tool use), human , and pending contracts. Swap an engine without touching the graph. Deterministic first Every workflow has a determinism profile and a worst-case token cost. Rules decide before models; an unavailable model is an error, never a silent fallback. Durable runs Runs survive restarts, wait for people, pause and resume on any worker, and compensate on rollback. Every run is journaled. Record, replay, test Pin any run as a fixture and replay it with zero tokens. Offline tests with typed mocks; calibrated, cached judges for free-text checks. Spec-driven Write intent in a spec; analysis proposes contracts and a task plan; codegen, validation and task status are deterministic. Coding agents use the same tools over MCP. Insight Specs and task board, a canvas over the same YAML, runs with breakpoints, step mode and approvals, change-engine checks, judge calibration. REST, SSE and MCP Typed OpenAPI from contracts, journal events over SSE, workflows as MCP tools, and a typed TypeScript client. Governed Ed25519-signed JWTs, default-deny triggers, approvals without self-approval, secure fields kept away from models, policy checked before you ship. Where to start ¶ Installation and the Quickstart The Agentic Manual — the complete document contract Spec-driven development and building with coding agents Engines , Runtime and journal , Insight AI agent instructions ¶ ⬇️ Download AGENTS.md — the rules for coding agents working in a tuvl project ⬇️ Download skills.zip — the tuvl 2.0 skill set (unzip to .agents/skills/ ; tuvl skills update does this for you) License ¶ tuvl is open source software licensed under the MIT license.

docs.text: Contributing ¶ Thank you for your interest in contributing to tuvl! Development setup ¶ Prerequisites ¶ Python 3.13 ( >=3.13,<3.14 ; see Installation → Troubleshooting ) uv PostgreSQL 16+ with pgvector, and Redis Node.js 20+ and pnpm (Insight) Install and run ¶ git clone https://github.com/tuvl-io/tuvl.git && cd tuvl uv sync --extra standard --group dev make ui-install uv run tuvl init demo --sample -y uv run tuvl dev -d demo --auto-login # Insight at http://localhost:8885/insight The repository's AGENTS.md maps the code: src/tuvl/contract/ (document model, type and expression languages), validate/ , runtime/ (durable runner, engines, journal), api/ (REST, SSE, MCP, dev API), spec/ , codegen/ , lock/ , testing/ , cli/ , core/ (config, models, auth, artifacts), and ui/ (Insight). Checks ¶ make check # ruff format + lint on src/ make typecheck-gate # mypy on the gated packages (must stay clean) TUVL_TEST_PG_URL=postgresql+asyncpg://tuvl:tuvl@localhost:5432/tuvl_test uv run pytest cd ui && pnpm exec tsc -b && pnpm test # Insight unit tests scripts/insight-smoke.sh # Insight browser tests (Playwright), needs a built UI and Postgres Tests that need Postgres skip without TUVL_TEST_PG_URL . CI runs all of the above. Changing behaviour ¶ The 2.0 specification is the contract: a change to a document kind, engine, signal or validation rule updates the schema ( contract/schema.py ), tuvl validate , codegen, Insight, the docs and the changelog together. Engines, document kinds and artifact types are closed sets — open an issue before proposing one. Add a test for every fix; prefer real Postgres over mocks for runtime behaviour. Keep comments to the non-obvious why . Pull Request Process ¶ Fork the repository Create a branch for your feature: git checkout -b feature/my-feature Make your changes with clear commit messages Add tests for new functionality Run tests to ensure everything passes Submit a PR with a clear description Commit Messages ¶ Use conventional commits: feat: add an http_<status> route for tool agents fix: decide rules type-check enum literals docs: update workflow configuration guide test: cover per-run transactions refactor: simplify repository pattern PR Description Template ¶ ## Description Brief description of changes ## Type of Change - [ ] Bug fix - [ ] New feature - [ ] Documentation update - [ ] Refactoring ## Testing - [ ] Unit tests added/updated - [ ] Integration tests pass - [ ] Manual testing performed ## Checklist - [ ] Code follows project style - [ ] Self-reviewed code - [ ] Documentation updated - [ ] No breaking changes (or documented) Documentation ¶ The site ( tuvl.dev ) is MkDocs Material in the docs repository. The engine's docs/*.md are the source of the Guide pages; make sync-internals copies them into the site. uv sync && uv run mkdocs serve uv run mkdocs build --strict Getting Help ¶ Issues : GitHub Issues Discussions : GitHub Discussions Discord : Join our Discord License ¶ By contributing, you agree that your contributions will be licensed under the MIT License.

There is no 1.x compatibility layer — 1.x workflows fail to load with an error pointing at the 2.0 format. The full list of changes is in the changelog . Highlights ¶ Typed agents, seven engines code , tool (db / http / mcp), decide , llm , loop , human , pending — one contract ( inputs , outputs , signals) for all of them. Named ends replace Response steps. Engines Checked before it runs tuvl validate checks contracts, data flow, types and policy (V001–V029) and prints each workflow's determinism profile and worst-case token cost. Agentic Manual Durable runtime Runs, journal and checkpoints in Postgres; leases so any worker continues any run; waits for people and tool approvals; compensation; pause, resume, abort, steer; replay. Runtime Rules first, models bounded decide evaluates rules before a decision model and never falls back silently; loop has hard budgets, per-tool approval and a supervisor; judges are calibrated and cached. Decide · Loop and tools · Judges Spec-driven The coding agent builds; tuvl referees. tuvl spec check checks the spec, tuvl spec verify checks the build against it, and task status is derived, never self-reported. tuvl codegen , tuvl test and tuvl lock are deterministic; tuvl mcp and 13 skills for coding agents. Spec-driven development Insight 2.0 Specs and task board, a canvas over the same YAML, runs with breakpoints and step mode, approvals, change-engine checks against pinned fixtures, judge calibration. Insight REST, SSE, MCP gRPC is gone. OpenAPI is generated from contracts; workflows can be exported as MCP tools; @tuvl/client 2.0 generates typed clients. API Ship and scale tuvl ship gates on validation and the lock and pins the engine version; the Helm chart can split API and worker pods. docs.text: Why tuvl ¶ Deterministic execution. Zero vibes. tuvl runs typed workflows of agents (code, database and HTTP tools, rules, models, bounded tool loops and people) on a durable, journaled runtime, built from specs. Every route is declared, every model call is budgeted and every run is recorded. The engine refuses anything the contract doesn't declare. This page holds the detail behind the four guarantees on tuvl.io : how execution, data and access are fenced, how tuvl compares with other tools, and what it means for each person who has to say yes. Workflow execution: every path is declared ¶ Seven engines, one contract. Every agent declares typed inputs , outputs and the signals it emits. Its engine is code , tool , decide , llm , loop , human or pending . Custom logic goes into a code agent (a typed Python function), not into the framework. Checked before it runs. tuvl validate applies 29 rules covering routes, data flow, types, expressions and policy. It prints each workflow's determinism profile and worst-case token cost. Every signal must be routed; there are no implicit edges. tuvl spec check and tuvl spec verify hold the build to its spec in the same way. Rules before models. A decide agent evaluates its rules first and asks a decision model only when none match. A typed-decision model such as self-hosted Laya returns calibrated probabilities, not text. An unavailable model is an error , never a silent fallback, and a doubtful answer routes low_confidence . Models stay bounded. llm and loop agents must declare token, time and iteration budgets. A model can only pick one of the routes you declared: its choice is constrained to the declared signals, and anything else routes parse_error . Every abnormal exit ( max_iterations , budget_exceeded , timeout , aborted ) is a routable signal. Loops are governed. Tools are agents, child workflows or allow-listed MCP tools, with schemas derived from their contracts. A risky call pauses for a person's approval, a supervisor can pause, steer or abort, and calibrated judges fail closed. Data and state: every access is fenced ¶ Agents see only their inputs. Undeclared context is invisible. An output that doesn't match the contract is a contract_violation , not a surprise further down the workflow. Model allowlist. A workflow can read and write only the models listed in spec.models . This is checked by the validator and again at runtime. Durable by default. Each step's writes commit with its checkpoint. A crashed worker's run resumes from the last checkpoint, and a rollback end compensates completed agents in reverse order. PII never reaches a model. Fields marked secure: true are refused as model inputs at validation, and redacted in the journal and in exports. Reproducible. tuvl.lock pins model ids, artifact hashes and MCP tool schemas. tuvl ship refuses a stale lock and pins the engine version. Security: fail closed, by construction ¶ Callers: no accidental public endpoints ¶ Deny by default. In production, every way to start a run requires a verified token: the workflow's route, the run API and MCP export. This holds even when the YAML declares no scope or group. Forgetting auth config doesn't open an endpoint; it locks one. Public is a declaration, not an omission. trigger.http.public: true is the only way to serve anonymous traffic. Combining it with a required scope or group is a validation error. Gated approvals. A person deciding a human step needs the approvals:decide scope and the step's required_group . On a group-gated step they can't be the person who started the run. Every decision is journaled with who made it. See IAM . Data: read and write are separate grants ¶ CRUD is opt-in. A model gets REST routes only for the operations it lists in spec.api.crud . read , write and delete are independent grants, carried as signed claims in offline-verifiable access tokens (Ed25519 JWTs). Group-pinned models. spec.access can restrict a model to named IAM groups per tier. A caller needs the scope and the membership; the only bypass is the explicit iam:admin grant. Restrictions cascade down, never up. Declare who may read, and the write and delete tiers inherit that fence unless you narrow them further. Surface: the API you don't declare doesn't exist ¶ Kill the CRUD plane entirely. One SystemConfig line unmounts every auto-generated /models/* route. The routes are absent from the router and the OpenAPI schema, rather than hidden behind a 403. No signing key, no boot. A production engine without its signing key refuses to start rather than fall back to anything weaker. Dev conveniences can't leak. The dev-mode superuser shortcut hard-exits the process if it's ever enabled in production. How tuvl compares ¶ Visual flow builders Langflow · Flowise · Dify Code-first frameworks LangGraph · CrewAI · Agents SDK tuvl Source of truth The canvas; exports are JSON blobs Your codebase Specs and YAML in git; Insight's canvas edits the same files What you ship A flow hosted inside the tool A library inside an app you still build A mounted API (routes, models, auth, telemetry), live the day the YAML merges When it breaks At runtime, inside the tool Wherever the Python throws Checked before it runs; declared failures route as signals; a crashed worker's run resumes from its last checkpoint Can the model invent a path? Components are open-ended The graph constrains it; the app around it is code No: it picks from the routes you declared Auth and tenancy The tool's API keys; the rest is yours Bring your own Scoped tokens per route; row-level tenancy Integrations Connector catalogs Ecosystems, plus whatever you write MCP tools in, workflows out as MCP tools; plain HTTP for everything else Lock-in and exit Flows live in the tool's format and runtime A library you can pin, fork or vendor (the cleanest exit here) A YAML dialect you adopt, whose majors land on your calendar too. MIT engine; your data stays in your Postgres Path to production Export, then host around it Your Dockerfile, your infra One command to a container and Helm chart ( tuvl ship ) Visual builders are a good canvas for a human exploring. Code-first frameworks are a good library inside an app you own. tuvl is the backend itself, declared. When the closed set isn't enough, a code agent drops to one typed Python function that stays inside the contract: its exits route through declared signals, and its database access stays allowlisted. Who it's for ¶ Engineers: a mechanism you can audit. Typed agent contracts and seven engines form a closed set, checked by 29 validation rules before anything runs. The stack is FastAPI, Postgres with pgvector, LiteLLM and OpenTelemetry. Durable runs are rows in your Postgres, with no extra workflow server and no torch or langchain dependency. Run tuvl dev on a laptop, and tuvl ship for a container and Helm chart. Start with the Agentic Manual . Product managers: scope that ships this sprint. Start from a spec in plain language. The task board's progress is derived from the project, not self-reported. human agents put sign-off inside the workflow: the run waits, durably, for days if needed, and the approval is on record. When someone asks "why did the AI do that?", you open the run and show them. Stakeholders: risk with a fence around it. MIT-licensed and open source, with no per-seat or per-call platform fee; the only spend is your own infrastructure and model tokens. Your data stays in your Postgres, PII marked secure never reaches a model, and decisions can run on a self-hosted model in your own cluster. The business logic is portable YAML and the runtime is a standard Python wheel, so adopting tuvl doesn't strand you in it. See it built ¶ The examples range from one typed model call (Invoice Extraction API) to durable human review (Content Moderation Pipeline) and a supervised investigation loop with a calibrated judge and group-gated compliance decisions (KYC Onboarding). Or run any of them in a throwaway sandbox at try.tuvl.online .

A model gets REST routes only for the operations it lists in spec.api.crud . read , write and delete are independent grants, carried as signed claims in offline-verifiable access tokens (Ed25519 JWTs). Group-pinned models. spec.access can restrict a model to named IAM groups per tier. A caller needs the scope and the membership; the only bypass is the explicit iam:admin grant. Restrictions cascade down, never up. Declare who may read, and the write and delete tiers inherit that fence unless you narrow them further.
docs.title: Data: read and write are separate grants

docs.text: Kill the CRUD plane entirely. One SystemConfig line unmounts every auto-generated /models/* route. The routes are absent from the router and the OpenAPI schema, rather than hidden behind a 403. No signing key, no boot. A production engine without its signing key refuses to start rather than fall back to anything weaker. Dev conveniences can't leak. The dev-mode superuser shortcut hard-exits the process if it's ever enabled in production.
docs.title: Surface: the API you don't declare doesn't exist

docs.text: Visual flow builders Langflow · Flowise · Dify Code-first frameworks LangGraph · CrewAI · Agents SDK tuvl Source of truth The canvas; exports are JSON blobs Your codebase Specs and YAML in git; Insight's canvas edits the same files What you ship A flow hosted inside the tool A library inside an app you still build A mounted API (routes, models, auth, telemetry), live the day the YAML merges When it breaks At runtime, inside the tool Wherever the Python throws Checked before it runs; declared failures route as signals; a crashed worker's run resumes from its last checkpoint Can the model invent a path? Components are open-ended The graph constrains it; the app around it is code No: it picks from the routes you declared Auth and tenancy The tool's API keys; the rest is yours Bring your own Scoped tokens per route; row-level tenancy Integrations Connector catalogs Ecosystems, plus whatever you write MCP tools in, workflows out as MCP tools; plain HTTP for everything else Lock-in and exit Flows live in the tool's format and runtime A library you can pin, fork or vendor (the cleanest exit here) A YAML dialect you adopt, whose majors land on your calendar too. MIT engine; your data stays in your Postgres Path to production Export, then host around it Your Dockerfile, your infra One command to a container and Helm chart ( tuvl ship ) Visual builders are a good canvas for a human exploring. Code-first frameworks are a good library inside an app you own. tuvl is the backend itself, declared. When the closed set isn't enough, a code agent drops to one typed Python function that stays inside the contract: its exits route through declared signals, and its database access stays allowlisted.
docs.title: How tuvl compares

docs.text: Engineers: a mechanism you can audit. Typed agent contracts and seven engines form a closed set, checked by 29 validation rules before anything runs. The stack is FastAPI, Postgres with pgvector, LiteLLM and OpenTelemetry. Durable runs are rows in your Postgres, with no extra workflow server and no torch or langchain dependency. Run tuvl dev on a laptop, and tuvl ship for a container and Helm chart. Start with the Agentic Manual . Product managers: scope that ships this sprint. Start from a spec in plain language. The task board's progress is derived from the project, not self-reported. human agents put sign-off inside the workflow: the run waits, durably, for days if needed, and the approval is on record. When someone asks "why did the AI do that?", you open the run and show them. Stakeholders: risk with a fence around it. MIT-licensed and open source, with no per-seat or per-call platform fee; the only spend is your own infrastructure and model tokens. Your data stays in your Postgres, PII marked secure never reaches a model, and decisions can run on a self-hosted model in your own cluster. The business logic is portable YAML and the runtime is a standard Python wheel, so adopting tuvl doesn't strand you in it.
docs.title: Who it's for

docs.text: The examples range from one typed model call (Invoice Extraction API) to durable human review (Content Moderation Pipeline) and a supervised investigation loop with a calibrated judge and group-gated compliance decisions (KYC Onboarding). Or run any of them in a throwaway sandbox at try.tuvl.online .

docs.text: AI Models ¶ An AgentModel (in llms/ ) names a model so workflows can refer to it. There are two types: llm (the default) for llm and loop agents, judges and spec analysis, and decision for the decide engine. tuvl init --preset gemini|openai|anthropic|ollama writes llms/default.yaml and llms/analysis.yaml for you. LLM models ¶ kind: AgentModel version: v1 metadata: name: default spec: model: gemini/gemini-3.1-flash-lite # a LiteLLM model id api_key: ${GEMINI_API_KEY} # optional; read from the environment temperature: 0.2 max_tokens: 2048 timeout: 60 Property Description model LiteLLM model id: provider/model (required) api_base Endpoint, for Ollama or a LiteLLM proxy api_key Use ${ENV_VAR} — secrets live in .env , never in YAML. Without it, the provider's standard variable ( OPENAI_API_KEY , ANTHROPIC_API_KEY , GEMINI_API_KEY , …) is used temperature , max_tokens Defaults for calls through this model (an agent's budget.max_tokens still bounds it) timeout Request timeout in seconds (default 60) enabled false disables the model; agents that use it fail loudly instead of falling back Provider Example model Ollama (local) ollama/llama3.1 with api_base: http://localhost:11434 OpenAI openai/gpt-5.4-mini Anthropic anthropic/claude-haiku-4-5 Gemini gemini/gemini-3.1-flash-lite LiteLLM proxy litellm_proxy/<name> with api_base and api_key Decision models ¶ kind: AgentModel metadata: { name: triage-classifier } spec: type: decision provider: litellm # laya | jev | litellm model: gemini/gemini-3.1-flash-lite A decision model picks one value of a decide agent's enum output with a confidence; it never writes free text. Laya (self-hosted). tuvl init --decision-model laya writes this model, LAYA_API_* entries in .env , and a compose.yaml that runs the laya-serve container on localhost:8000 ( docker compose up -d laya ). tuvl ship adds Laya to the Helm chart ( Shipping to production ). The tuvl/laya-serve image comes in two variants: Tag Checkpoints Memory Use with <version>-en english about 2 GiB model: english <version> english + multilingual about 3.5 GiB model: auto or multilingual tuvl init scaffolds model: english with the -en image, and tuvl ship picks the image (and the Helm memory requests) that matches the model. An -en image has no multilingual weights and runs offline, so non-English text sent to it fails with HTTP 500 inference failed — set model: auto and use the full image when you need other languages. kind: AgentModel metadata: { name: laya } spec: type: decision provider: laya model: english # english | auto | multilingual | typed-decisions api_base: ${LAYA_API_BASE:http://localhost:8000} api_key: ${LAYA_API_KEY:} # optional; an ${ENV_VAR} reference, never a literal key Jev (hosted). provider: jev with its api_base , and model pinned to a version ( jev-1.13.0 ). OpenAI-compatible endpoints (a LiteLLM proxy, your own classifier) use provider: litellm with model: openai/<name> , api_base and an ${ENV_VAR} api_key . The endpoint must return {"decision": …, "confidence": 0..1} (or token logprobs); an answer with no confidence is an error, never treated as certain. See Decide . Where models are used ¶ Site Field llm agent llm.model: default (or a LiteLLM id directly) loop agent loop.model decide agent decide.model.ref — a decision model or an llm model Judge artifact spec.model Model ids are pinned in tuvl.lock by tuvl lock . You can also manage models on the Insight AI Models page.

docs.text: Datasource Configuration ¶ Datasources define database connections for your tuvl application. PostgreSQL Configuration ¶ kind: "DataSource" version: "v1" metadata: name: "main_postgres" primary: true spec: type: "postgresql" driver: "asyncpg" connection: host: "${POSTGRES_HOST}" port: ${POSTGRES_PORT:5432} database: "${POSTGRES_DB}" username: "${POSTGRES_USER}" password: "${POSTGRES_PASSWORD}" pooling: min_size: 5 max_size: 20 Metadata Properties ¶ Property Type Required Description name string Yes Unique identifier for this datasource primary boolean No Mark this as the primary datasource. System tables (IAM, HITL, vector store) and the bootstrap ledger are created here. Only one datasource should be marked primary; if none is marked, the first Postgres datasource loaded is used automatically. Connection Properties ¶ Property Type Required Description host string Yes Database server hostname port integer No Port number (default: 5432) database string Yes Database name username string Yes Connection username password string Yes Connection password Pool Configuration ¶ Property Type Default Description min_size integer 5 Minimum connections to maintain max_size integer 20 Maximum connections allowed Tuning Guidelines ¶ Development : min_size: 2 , max_size: 10 Production : min_size: 5-10 , max_size: 20-50 Keep min_size low to reduce idle resource usage Set max_size based on expected concurrent requests Environment Variables ¶ Create a .env file: POSTGRES_HOST=localhost POSTGRES_PORT=5432 POSTGRES_DB=tuvl POSTGRES_USER=postgres POSTGRES_PASSWORD=your_secret_password And a .env.example for documentation: POSTGRES_HOST=localhost POSTGRES_PORT=5432 POSTGRES_DB=tuvl POSTGRES_USER=postgres POSTGRES_PASSWORD= Multiple Databases ¶ Define multiple datasources for different purposes: kind: "DataSource" version: "v1" metadata: name: "primary" spec: type: "postgresql" driver: "asyncpg" connection: host: "${PRIMARY_DB_HOST}" database: "${PRIMARY_DB_NAME}" username: "${PRIMARY_DB_USER}" password: "${PRIMARY_DB_PASSWORD}" kind: "DataSource" version: "v1" metadata: name: "analytics" spec: type: "postgresql" driver: "asyncpg" connection: host: "${ANALYTICS_DB_HOST}" database: "${ANALYTICS_DB_NAME}" username: "${ANALYTICS_DB_USER}" password: "${ANALYTICS_DB_PASSWORD}" SSL/TLS Configuration ¶ For secure connections: spec: type: "postgresql" driver: "asyncpg" connection: host: "${POSTGRES_HOST}" port: 5432 database: "${POSTGRES_DB}" username: "${POSTGRES_USER}" password: "${POSTGRES_PASSWORD}" ssl: mode: "require" # disable, allow, prefer, require, verify-ca, verify-full ca_cert: "/path/to/ca.crt" Docker Compose Example ¶ version: "3.8" services: postgres: image: postgres:16-alpine environment: POSTGRES_USER: postgres POSTGRES_PASSWORD: postgres POSTGRES_DB: tuvl ports: - "5432:5432" volumes: - postgres_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data app: build: . environment: POSTGRES_HOST: postgres POSTGRES_PORT: 5432 POSTGRES_DB: tuvl POSTGRES_USER: postgres POSTGRES_PASSWORD: postgres depends_on: - postgres volumes: postgres_data: Connection String Format ¶ Internally, tuvl builds a connection string: postgresql+asyncpg://user:password@host:port/database Troubleshooting ¶ Connection Refused ¶ sqlalchemy.exc.OperationalError: connection refused Check PostgreSQL is running: pg_isready -h localhost Verify hostname and port Check firewall rules Authentication Failed ¶ asyncpg.exceptions.InvalidPasswordError: password authentication failed Verify username and password Check pg_hba.conf authentication settings Database Does Not Exist ¶ asyncpg.exceptions.InvalidCatalogNameError: database "tuvl" does not exist Create the database: createdb tuvl # or psql -c "CREATE DATABASE tuvl;" Pool Exhausted ¶ asyncpg.exceptions.TooManyConnectionsError Increase max_size in pool config Check for connection leaks (unclosed sessions) Add connection timeout handling Best Practices ¶ 1. Never Commit Secrets ¶ .env *.pem *.key 2. Use Environment Variables ¶ # Good password: "${POSTGRES_PASSWORD}" # Never do this password: "hardcoded_password" 3. Set Reasonable Pool Limits ¶ pooling: min_size: 5 # Low enough for idle efficiency max_size: 20 # High enough for peak load 4. Use SSL in Production ¶ ssl: mode: "verify-full" ca_cert: "${SSL_CA_PATH}" Redis Configuration ¶ Redis is a second supported datasource type used for distributed state — specifically OAuth CSRF tokens and the token revocation blacklist. kind: DataSource version: v1 metadata: name: redis-primary spec: type: redis connection: host: ${REDIS_HOST:localhost} port: ${REDIS_PORT:6379} db: 0 password: ${REDIS_PASSWORD:} # leave blank for no authentication Redis Connection Properties ¶ Property Type Default Description host string localhost Redis server hostname port integer 6379 Redis server port db integer 0 Database index (0–15) password string (none) AUTH password; omit for unauthenticated connections Selection logic When multiple type: redis datasource files exist, tuvl picks the one that sorts first alphabetically by filename. Name your primary Redis file redis-primary.yaml or 00-redis.yaml to ensure predictable selection. Multi-worker requirement Without a configured and reachable Redis datasource, OAuth state tokens and the token revocation blacklist fall back to in-process memory. This is only safe for single-worker development. For production multi-worker deployments Redis is required . For full details on scaling considerations and Docker setup, see Redis Configuration . Next Steps ¶ Redis — Configure Redis for distributed state Agents — Configure LLM providers Agentic Manual — documents, types and models

docs.text: Configuration Overview ¶ tuvl uses YAML files for all configuration. This keeps your logic declarative and version-controllable. Configuration Types ¶ Kind Directory Purpose ModelDefinition models/ Data model schemas Workflow workflows/ Business logic flows DataSource datasources/ Database connections AgentModel agents/ LLM provider presets Artifact artifacts/ Named, versioned assets — prompts, steering, skills, guardrails, hooks, MCP servers — referenced via artifact://name[@version] SystemConfig .tuvl/system.yaml Project-level, boot-time API surface settings Environment Variables ¶ Sensitive values use environment variable substitution: connection: host: "${POSTGRES_HOST}" password: "${POSTGRES_PASSWORD}" Syntax ¶ Pattern Behavior ${VAR} Required — fails if not set ${VAR:default} Optional — uses default if not set ${VAR:-default} Same as above (alternate syntax) Example ¶ spec: connection: host: "${POSTGRES_HOST}" # Required port: ${POSTGRES_PORT:5432} # Default: 5432 database: "${POSTGRES_DB:-tuvl}" # Default: tuvl File Organization ¶ project/ ├── .env # Secret values (git-ignored) ├── .env.example # Template (safe to commit) ├── models/ │ ├── user.yaml │ └── order.yaml ├── workflows/ │ ├── onboarding.yaml │ └── checkout.yaml ├── datasources/ │ └── postgres.yaml └── agents/ └── default.yaml Common Patterns ¶ YAML Anchors ¶ Reduce duplication with anchors: agents: - id: summarise # … budget: &llm_budget { timeout: 30s, max_tokens: 1500, retry: { attempts: 2, errors: [timeout, parse_error] } } - id: reply # … budget: *llm_budget Define the anchor where it is first used: documents are strict, so an extra top-level key just to hold an anchor is rejected. Multi-Document Files ¶ tuvl reads each YAML document separately using yaml.safe_load_all . This lets you pack multiple definitions into a single file — useful for colocating related versions: # models/all.yaml kind: "ModelDefinition" metadata: name: "User" schema_version: "v1" spec: tablename: "users" # ... --- kind: "ModelDefinition" metadata: name: "User" schema_version: "v2" # new version in same file enabled: false # staged — activate via admin API spec: tablename: "users" # ... The same pattern works for Workflow documents. Every version — enabled or disabled — is stored in the corresponding *_VERSION_REGISTRY so the admin API can list, toggle, and fork it. schema_version ¶ metadata.schema_version tags a definition with a version string. It defaults to "v1" when omitted. Multiple definitions sharing the same metadata.name but different schema_version values coexist in the registry independently. enabled ¶ Setting enabled: false excludes a definition from active use (no route mounted, no CRUD endpoints) but keeps it visible and manageable through the admin API. Omitting the field is equivalent to enabled: true . SystemConfig ( .tuvl/system.yaml ) ¶ Boot-time settings that shape the mounted API surface, read once at startup. The only knob today is spec.api.expose_model_crud : kind: SystemConfig metadata: name: system spec: api: expose_model_crud: false # default: true Setting expose_model_crud: false unmounts every auto-generated /models/* CRUD router — the routes are absent entirely, not merely scope-denied — leaving only hand-authored Workflow triggers exposed. Restart required for the change to take effect. TUVL_EXPOSE_MODEL_CRUD overrides the YAML value at the env level (env wins over .tuvl/system.yaml ). In dev mode, the toggle is also editable from the Insight Settings page 's API Access section. See Authorization Surfaces for the CRUD and workflow-trigger auth model this knob sits alongside. Validation ¶ tuvl validates configurations at startup. Invalid files are logged and skipped: INFO: 📋 Model loaded: 'User' WARNING: ⚠️ models/broken.yaml: missing required field 'spec.tablename' — skipped INFO: 📋 Model loaded: 'Order' Hot Reloading (Development) ¶ In development mode, configuration changes are detected: tuvl dev --reload Production Disable hot reloading in production for stability. Next Steps ¶ Datasources — Database configuration Agents — LLM provider setup

docs.text: Boot-time settings that shape the mounted API surface, read once at startup. The only knob today is spec.api.expose_model_crud : kind: SystemConfig metadata: name: system spec: api: expose_model_crud: false # default: true Setting expose_model_crud: false unmounts every auto-generated /models/* CRUD router — the routes are absent entirely, not merely scope-denied — leaving only hand-authored Workflow triggers exposed. Restart required for the change to take effect. TUVL_EXPOSE_MODEL_CRUD overrides the YAML value at the env level (env wins over .tuvl/system.yaml ). In dev mode, the toggle is also editable from the Insight Settings page 's API Access section. See Authorization Surfaces for the CRUD and workflow-trigger auth model this knob sits alongside.

docs.text: Redis Configuration ¶ Redis is an optional but strongly recommended infrastructure dependency for tuvl. It is used for: Feature Without Redis With Redis OAuth CSRF state tokens In-process dict (single worker only) Shared across all workers Token revocation blacklist In-process dict (single worker only) Shared across all workers When Is Redis Required? ¶ Redis is required for any multi-worker or multi-process deployment. If you run more than one tuvl worker (e.g. tuvl run --workers 4 ), there is no shared memory between processes. Without Redis: An OAuth callback routed to a different worker than the one that generated the state will always fail the CSRF check. A token revoked via POST /auth/logout on one worker will still be accepted by all other workers. In single-worker tuvl dev mode Redis is optional — the in-process fallback is sufficient. Configuration ¶ Create a YAML file in your project's datasources/ directory: kind: DataSource version: v1 metadata: name: redis-primary spec: type: redis connection: host: ${REDIS_HOST:localhost} port: ${REDIS_PORT:6379} db: 0 password: ${REDIS_PASSWORD:} # empty string → no AUTH command sent tuvl picks up the first type: redis datasource (sorted alphabetically by name) and attempts to connect at startup. Connection Properties ¶ Property Type Default Description host string localhost Redis server hostname or IP port integer 6379 Redis server port db integer 0 Database index (0–15) password string (none) AUTH password; omit or leave blank for no auth Environment Variables ¶ REDIS_HOST=redis.internal REDIS_PORT=6379 REDIS_PASSWORD=your-redis-password # optional Environment Variable Syntax ¶ The ${VAR:default} syntax used in the YAML is resolved before connecting: Pattern Behaviour ${REDIS_HOST:localhost} Uses REDIS_HOST env var; falls back to localhost ${REDIS_PASSWORD:} Uses REDIS_PASSWORD env var; falls back to empty string (no auth) ${REDIS_HOST} Requires REDIS_HOST to be set — fails startup with a clear error if missing Startup Behaviour ¶ When tuvl starts, it logs one of the following: 🟥 Redis connected: localhost:6379 db=0 (datasource: 'redis-primary') or, if no datasource is configured or connection fails: ℹ️ No Redis datasource configured — OAuth state and token blacklist will use in-process memory (not suitable for multi-worker deployments). or, if the datasource is configured but the server is unreachable: ⚠️ Redis datasource 'redis-primary' (localhost:6379) is unreachable: ... — falling back to in-process memory. tuvl never fails to start due to Redis being unavailable. The fallback is automatic. Redis availability is checked at the point of use via is_redis_available() . Using Redis for Other Purposes ¶ The Redis client is accessible in application code for custom caching or messaging: from tuvl.core.infra.redis import get_redis_client, is_redis_available async def my_function(): if is_redis_available(): redis = get_redis_client() await redis.set("my:key", "value", ex=300) else: # fallback path ... Docker Setup ¶ services: redis: image: redis:7-alpine ports: - "6379:6379" command: redis-server --requirepass "${REDIS_PASSWORD}" volumes: - redis_data:/data tuvl: # ... environment: REDIS_HOST: redis REDIS_PASSWORD: "${REDIS_PASSWORD}" depends_on: - redis volumes: redis_data: Managed Redis Services ¶ Provider Notes AWS ElastiCache Set host to the primary endpoint; use password for auth token Redis Cloud Standard connection; enable TLS if required (not yet built-in; use a tunnel) Upstash REST API not supported; use the standard TCP endpoint Render / Railway Use the internal REDIS_URL ; parse host/port/password from it manually Azure Cache for Redis Use non-TLS port 6379 for simplicity or configure a TLS proxy UI Configuration ¶ Redis can be configured directly from the tuvl UI: Navigate to Settings → Infrastructure → Redis Fill in the host, port, db index, and optional password Click Save — the YAML file will be written to datasources/redis-primary.yaml The status badge shows Configured when the file exists. The actual Redis connectivity is only visible in the server logs at startup.

docs.text: Example projects ¶ The tuvl-io/examples repository holds complete tuvl 2.0 projects. Each example is a complete 2.0 project: a spec in specs/ with acceptance examples, generated offline tests, a tuvl.lock , and the CI gate wired up. Each runs with tuvl dev and can be tried in a browser sandbox at try.tuvl.online . Example What it shows Engines sentiment-api Classify a product review and persist it — the smallest useful workflow llm , tool (db) invoice-extraction-api Extract a structured invoice from text, verify it deterministically, persist it; per-signal outputs (valid / mismatch / incomplete) llm , code , tool content-moderation-pipeline Classify user content, apply region policy in code, notify a channel, and send borderline items to a person llm , code , tool (http), human knowledge-base-qa Retrieval-augmented answers with citations on the built-in vector rails code ( tuvl.data_ingest , tuvl.data_search ), llm support-triage Rules-first triage ( decide ), an investigating loop with a supervisor, and a tool call that needs approval before issuing a credit (a child workflow) decide , loop , llm , tool , code mcp-research-agent A bounded loop driving an MCP fetch server (allow-listed tools, schema pinned in tuvl.lock ) to write a cited brief loop , tool (mcp), llm , code kyc-onboarding PII-safe intake ( secure: true ), sanctions screening, a supervised investigation loop with a calibrated judge , and a compliance officer's decision loop , human , llm , tool , code git clone https://github.com/tuvl-io/examples && cd examples/support-triage cp .env.example .env # add a model key and Postgres settings tuvl validate --strict tuvl dev --auto-login

docs.text: Code generation ¶ tuvl codegen writes the parts of a project that follow mechanically from its YAML, so you only write the parts that need judgement. It is deterministic: no model is called, and tuvl never writes function bodies . tuvl codegen # all workflows tuvl codegen triage_ticket # one workflow's stubs, prompts and tests tuvl codegen --check # write nothing; exit 1 if anything would change (the CI gate) What it generates ¶ Output Rule agents/_generated/schemas.py <Id>In / <Id>Out models per agent (per-signal variants and <Id>Signal ), plus <Workflow>Input and <Workflow>End . Never hand-edited agents/<run>.py A stub for each code agent when missing; when present, a merge that refreshes the decorator, signature and docstring and keeps your body artifacts/<name>.md A prompt placeholder for an artifact:// that an llm or loop agent references and that does not exist yet decide agents A block with neither rules nor a model gets one never-matching rule per enum value, each marked # TODO tests/<workflow>/<example>.yaml A test per tuvl-example block in the spec. Hand-written tests are never touched The loop for a code agent ¶ Declare the agent in the workflow YAML (or add a step in Insight): its run , inputs , outputs . Run tuvl codegen . You get a typed stub: from __future__ import annotations from tuvl import Ctx, agent from agents._generated.schemas import ScoreTicketIn, ScoreTicketOut @agent("score_ticket") async def score_ticket(inp: ScoreTicketIn, ctx: Ctx) -> ScoreTicketOut: """Score how urgent a ticket is.""" raise NotImplementedError("score_ticket") Replace the raise with your logic. Everything above the body is owned by codegen. Change the contract later (rename an input, add an output) and run tuvl codegen again: the signature and types update, and your body stays. In Insight, choosing the code engine for an agent offers ⌘ Generate stub , which runs the same step, and saving the Python file normalizes the decorator and signature through codegen. Keeping it honest in CI ¶ Generated files are committed, so a contract change that was not regenerated is a failing build: tuvl codegen --check It is one step of the CI gate , alongside tuvl validate --strict , tuvl lock --check and tuvl test --strict . Run tuvl codegen locally and commit the result. Notes ¶ Don't edit agents/_generated/ . It is rewritten on every run. One @agent("run") per contract. If two agents share a run with different contracts, codegen warns and types the function as Any . Coding agents can run it through the dev MCP server: codegen (a dry run) always, and codegen_write with --allow-write . See Build with Coding Agents . See also ¶ Spec-driven development — where codegen sits in the flow Project structure CLI reference

docs.text: Build with coding agents ¶ tuvl is designed so a coding agent (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Kiro, …) can build a project from a spec without guessing: tuvl tells it the state of the project, and deterministic tools do everything except the parts that need judgement. What a project gives the agent ¶ AGENTS.md at the root and skills in .agents/skills/ (mirrored to .claude/skills/ ), scaffolded by tuvl init and refreshed with tuvl skills update [--diff] : Skill Use it when tuvl-spec writing or changing specs/<name>.md tuvl-plan turning a spec into contracts and tasks tuvl-task-loop always — the core loop for implementing tasks agent-code / agent-tool / agent-llm / agent-loop / agent-decide / agent-human implementing an agent with that engine tuvl-data models, fields, access, CRUD tuvl-test tests, mocks, fixtures, judges tuvl-harden changing a working workflow safely tuvl-ship lock, CI gate, shipping --json on every read command ( validate , spec status , spec diff , test , runs , …), with documented schemas. tuvl mcp — the same operations as MCP tools over stdio. Connect tuvl mcp ¶ { "mcpServers": { "tuvl": { "command": "tuvl", "args": ["mcp", "-d", "."] } } } Read tools: validate , spec_status , spec_diff , get_contract , list_agents , explain_error , get_run , get_run_events , plus dry runs of spec_analyse , codegen and test . Add --allow-write for spec_apply , codegen_write , run_workflow and pin_fixture . Run tools talk to a running server through TUVL_URL / TUVL_TOKEN . tuvl mcp refuses to run in production. The loop ¶ tuvl spec status --json → the next unblocked task and its target. tuvl codegen → typed schemas and stubs for the target. Implement: the YAML engine block, or the body of a code agent's function. tuvl validate --json → fix every error on the target. tuvl test → the task moves to tested , then done . Repeat until tuvl spec status --strict passes. Task statuses are derived from the project — an agent never sets them. Generated files ( agents/_generated/ , generated tests, tuvl.lock ) are regenerated, never edited. Downloads ¶ AGENTS.md and skills.zip for agents working outside a tuvl init project.
docs.title: Build with Coding Agents

docs.text: Installation ¶ This guide walks you through installing tuvl and its dependencies. Prerequisites ¶ Before installing tuvl, ensure you have: Python 3.13 or 3.14 — tuvl 2.0 supports >=3.13,<3.15 . uv picks a compatible interpreter automatically. uv — Fast Python package manager (recommended) PostgreSQL — For data persistence (optional for development) Docker — Optional. The easiest way to run PostgreSQL, Redis and Laya locally, and required by tuvl ship to build the production image Redis — Optional for tuvl dev ; needed when you run more than one worker ( why ) Laya ( tuvl/laya-serve ) — Optional. A self-hosted decision model for decide agents; runs as its own container Ollama — For local LLM inference (optional) What you actually need To try tuvl you need Python and uv, and a PostgreSQL database. Everything else above is opt-in: Redis only matters for multi-worker deployments, and Laya only if a decide agent uses it as its decision model. Python 3.14 tuvl 1.x was held to Python 3.13 because its token library ( biscuit-python ) had no 3.14 builds. tuvl 2.0 signs tokens as standard JWTs and runs on 3.13 and 3.14 on Linux, macOS and Windows. Installing uv ¶ macOS / Linux Windows pip curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh powershell -c "irm https://astral.sh/uv/install.ps1 | iex" pip install uv 2.0 public beta ¶ tuvl 2.0.0 is released on 20 October 2026 . Until then, 2.0 is available as the public beta 2.0.0b3 . A plain uv tool install tuvl still installs the latest 1.x release, so ask for the beta explicitly: # CLI + dev server + Insight (recommended) uv tool install --prerelease allow "tuvl[standard]==2.0.0b3" # CLI only uv tool install "tuvl==2.0.0b3" --prerelease allow is needed because uv only takes a pre-release for packages you name yourself, and tuvl[standard] pulls in tuvl-insight 2.0.0b3 indirectly. The TypeScript client has a matching beta on npm's beta channel: npm install @tuvl/client@beta # 2.0.0-beta.1 From 20 October the commands below install 2.0.0 directly. Report beta issues on GitHub . Installing tuvl CLI ¶ Install the tuvl CLI globally using uv: # Base CLI only uv tool install tuvl # With dev server and built-in UI (recommended) uv tool install "tuvl[standard]" Tip tuvl[standard] includes the dev server ( tuvl dev ), the built-in tuvl insight UI, and hot-reload support. Use the base install for production-only deployments where the UI is not needed. Verify the installation: tuvl --version Installing tuvl as a Project Dependency ¶ For projects that embed the engine directly: # Base engine uv add tuvl # With dev server and built-in UI uv add "tuvl[standard]" Or with pip: pip install "tuvl[standard]" Optional Dependencies ¶ PostgreSQL ¶ macOS (Homebrew) Ubuntu/Debian Docker brew install postgresql@16 brew services start postgresql@16 sudo apt update sudo apt install postgresql postgresql-contrib sudo systemctl start postgresql docker run -d \ --name tuvl-postgres \ -e POSTGRES_USER=postgres \ -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=postgres \ -e POSTGRES_DB=tuvl \ -p 5432:5432 \ postgres:16-alpine Redis (optional) ¶ Redis shares OAuth state and the token-revocation list between workers. A single tuvl dev process works without it (an in-process fallback is used); add it before running more than one worker. See Redis configuration for the datasource file. macOS (Homebrew) Ubuntu/Debian Docker brew install redis brew services start redis sudo apt install redis-server sudo systemctl start redis-server docker run -d --name tuvl-redis -p 6379:6379 redis:7-alpine Then add datasources/redis-primary.yaml with type: redis , host: ${REDIS_HOST:localhost} . Laya decision server (optional) ¶ Laya is an open-weight model that picks one value of a decide agent's enum with a confidence. It runs on CPU in its own container, offline, with verified weights baked in. Use it when you want decisions made on your own infrastructure instead of calling a hosted model. The quickest route is to let tuvl init scaffold it: tuvl init my-project --decision-model laya -y cd my-project docker compose up -d laya # serves on http://localhost:8000 This writes llms/laya.yaml (a provider: laya AgentModel), LAYA_API_* entries in .env and a compose.yaml . To run the container by hand: English only (smaller) English + multilingual docker run -d --name laya -p 127.0.0.1:8000:8000 tuvl/laya-serve:0.4.7-1-en docker run -d --name laya -p 127.0.0.1:8000:8000 tuvl/laya-serve:0.4.7-1 Image Use with Memory …-en model: english about 2 GiB full model: auto or multilingual about 3.5 GiB The image is about 2.7 GB (CPU PyTorch plus the weights), amd64 and arm64. Check it is up with curl localhost:8000/health . Details, checkpoints and settings are in AI Models → Laya and Decide . Ollama (Local LLM) ¶ macOS Linux Docker brew install ollama ollama serve # In another terminal, pull a model ollama pull llama3 curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh | sh ollama serve # In another terminal ollama pull llama3 docker run -d \ --name ollama \ -p 11434:11434 \ -v ollama:/root/.ollama \ ollama/ollama docker exec ollama ollama pull llama3 Verifying Installation ¶ Create the sample project and run its checks: tuvl init my-project --sample --preset gemini -y # or openai | anthropic | ollama cd my-project tuvl validate --strict tuvl test tuvl dev --auto-login tuvl dev serves the engine on port 8885 and Insight at http://127.0.0.1:8885/insight/ . With --auto-login this machine skips the key screen; otherwise paste the session key, stored in .tuvl/.dev-session ( tuvl dev --show-key prints it). Troubleshooting ¶ Windows: port already in use or permission denied ¶ Symptom — tuvl dev fails to start the engine on its default port ( 8885 ) with one of: [Errno 48] Address already in use / Only one usage of each socket address … is normally permitted PermissionError: [WinError 10013] An attempt was made to access a socket in a way forbidden by its access permissions Why this happens — either another process is already bound to the port, or — common on Windows — the port falls inside a range Windows has reserved for dynamic allocation. Hyper-V, WSL 2, and Docker Desktop routinely reserve large TCP ranges; binding a port inside a reserved range fails with WinError 10013 even though nothing is actively listening on it. Inspect the reserved ranges: netsh interface ipv4 show excludedportrange protocol=tcp If 8885 sits inside an excluded range (or is otherwise taken), run tuvl on a free port: One-off flag Environment variable tuvl dev --port 8899 # Persist a different port for all tuvl commands in this shell $env:TUVL_DEV_PORT = "8899" tuvl dev Tip The port also appears in the login URL tuvl prints ( http://127.0.0.1:<port>/insight/ ). If you rely on the OAuth callback flow, align TUVL_OAUTH_BASE_URL with the port you chose (defaults to http://localhost:8885 ). The default 8885 spells T·U·V·L on a phone keypad and deliberately avoids the crowded 8000 / 8080 / 8888 range — but any free, non-reserved port works. Next Steps ¶ Quickstart Guide — Build your first workflow Code generation — tuvl codegen : typed schemas, stubs and tests Shipping to production — tuvl ship : image, Helm chart, Laya and secrets Project Structure — Understand the project layout Agentic Manual — how tuvl projects are written

docs.text: This guide walks you through installing tuvl and its dependencies.
docs.title: Installation

docs.text: Before installing tuvl, ensure you have: Python 3.13 or 3.14 — tuvl 2.0 supports >=3.13,<3.15 . uv picks a compatible interpreter automatically. uv — Fast Python package manager (recommended) PostgreSQL — For data persistence (optional for development) Docker — Optional. The easiest way to run PostgreSQL, Redis and Laya locally, and required by tuvl ship to build the production image Redis — Optional for tuvl dev ; needed when you run more than one worker ( why ) Laya ( tuvl/laya-serve ) — Optional. A self-hosted decision model for decide agents; runs as its own container Ollama — For local LLM inference (optional) What you actually need To try tuvl you need Python and uv, and a PostgreSQL database. Everything else above is opt-in: Redis only matters for multi-worker deployments, and Laya only if a decide agent uses it as its decision model. Python 3.14 tuvl 1.x was held to Python 3.13 because its token library ( biscuit-python ) had no 3.14 builds. tuvl 2.0 signs tokens as standard JWTs and runs on 3.13 and 3.14 on Linux, macOS and Windows.
docs.title: Prerequisites

docs.text: macOS / Linux Windows pip curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh powershell -c "irm https://astral.sh/uv/install.ps1 | iex" pip install uv
docs.title: Installing uv

docs.text: tuvl 2.0.0 is released on 20 October 2026 . Until then, 2.0 is available as the public beta 2.0.0b3 . A plain uv tool install tuvl still installs the latest 1.x release, so ask for the beta explicitly: # CLI + dev server + Insight (recommended) uv tool install --prerelease allow "tuvl[standard]==2.0.0b3" # CLI only uv tool install "tuvl==2.0.0b3" --prerelease allow is needed because uv only takes a pre-release for packages you name yourself, and tuvl[standard] pulls in tuvl-insight 2.0.0b3 indirectly. The TypeScript client has a matching beta on npm's beta channel: npm install @tuvl/client@beta # 2.0.0-beta.1 From 20 October the commands below install 2.0.0 directly. Report beta issues on GitHub .
docs.title: 2.0 public beta

docs.text: Install the tuvl CLI globally using uv: # Base CLI only uv tool install tuvl # With dev server and built-in UI (recommended) uv tool install "tuvl[standard]" Tip tuvl[standard] includes the dev server ( tuvl dev ), the built-in tuvl insight UI, and hot-reload support. Use the base install for production-only deployments where the UI is not needed. Verify the installation: tuvl --version
docs.title: Installing tuvl CLI

docs.text: For projects that embed the engine directly: # Base engine uv add tuvl # With dev server and built-in UI uv add "tuvl[standard]" Or with pip: pip install "tuvl[standard]"
docs.title: Installing tuvl as a Project Dependency

docs.text: macOS (Homebrew) Ubuntu/Debian Docker brew install postgresql@16 brew services start postgresql@16 sudo apt update sudo apt install postgresql postgresql-contrib sudo systemctl start postgresql docker run -d \ --name tuvl-postgres \ -e POSTGRES_USER=postgres \ -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=postgres \ -e POSTGRES_DB=tuvl \ -p 5432:5432 \ postgres:16-alpine
docs.title: PostgreSQL

docs.text: Redis shares OAuth state and the token-revocation list between workers. A single tuvl dev process works without it (an in-process fallback is used); add it before running more than one worker. See Redis configuration for the datasource file. macOS (Homebrew) Ubuntu/Debian Docker brew install redis brew services start redis sudo apt install redis-server sudo systemctl start redis-server docker run -d --name tuvl-redis -p 6379:6379 redis:7-alpine Then add datasources/redis-primary.yaml with type: redis , host: ${REDIS_HOST:localhost} .
docs.title: Redis (optional)

docs.text: Laya is an open-weight model that picks one value of a decide agent's enum with a confidence. It runs on CPU in its own container, offline, with verified weights baked in. Use it when you want decisions made on your own infrastructure instead of calling a hosted model. The quickest route is to let tuvl init scaffold it: tuvl init my-project --decision-model laya -y cd my-project docker compose up -d laya # serves on http://localhost:8000 This writes llms/laya.yaml (a provider: laya AgentModel), LAYA_API_* entries in .env and a compose.yaml . To run the container by hand: English only (smaller) English + multilingual docker run -d --name laya -p 127.0.0.1:8000:8000 tuvl/laya-serve:0.4.7-1-en docker run -d --name laya -p 127.0.0.1:8000:8000 tuvl/laya-serve:0.4.7-1 Image Use with Memory …-en model: english about 2 GiB full model: auto or multilingual about 3.5 GiB The image is about 2.7 GB (CPU PyTorch plus the weights), amd64 and arm64. Check it is up with curl localhost:8000/health . Details, checkpoints and settings are in AI Models → Laya and Decide .
docs.title: Laya decision server (optional)

docs.text: macOS Linux Docker brew install ollama ollama serve # In another terminal, pull a model ollama pull llama3 curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh | sh ollama serve # In another terminal ollama pull llama3 docker run -d \ --name ollama \ -p 11434:11434 \ -v ollama:/root/.ollama \ ollama/ollama docker exec ollama ollama pull llama3

docs.text: Create the sample project and run its checks: tuvl init my-project --sample --preset gemini -y # or openai | anthropic | ollama cd my-project tuvl validate --strict tuvl test tuvl dev --auto-login tuvl dev serves the engine on port 8885 and Insight at http://127.0.0.1:8885/insight/ . docs.text: Quickstart ¶ This walks through the sample project: a support-ticket triage workflow with a spec, a task list, tests and a lock that pass the CI gate as created. During the 2.0 beta, install tuvl as shown in Installation first. 1. Create the project ¶ tuvl init triage --sample --preset gemini -y # or openai | anthropic | ollama cd triage The preset writes llms/default.yaml (the agents' model) and reads the API key from your environment into .env . Point .env at a PostgreSQL database ( POSTGRES_* ). 2. Check it ¶ tuvl validate --strict triage_ticket 4 agents · 2 deterministic · 1 bounded · 1 external · worst-case 500 tok ✓ Validation passed Every workflow gets a determinism profile and a worst-case token cost . Then run the tests — offline, with recorded and mocked results: tuvl test tuvl spec status # every task derived as done 3. Open Insight ¶ tuvl dev --auto-login # http://localhost:8885/insight Workflows → triage_ticket shows the graph: classify (llm) → prioritise → review (human) → store (tool). Click a card to see its contract and engine. ▶ Run with a ticket. An urgent one stops at review : the Runs page shows the approval form; approve it and the run continues to store . 📌 Pin as fixture turns the run into a test that replays with zero tokens. 4. Call it ¶ curl -X POST localhost:8885/api/tickets/triage \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"subject": "Refund", "body": "I was charged twice", "customer_email": "a@example.com"}' The response is the end's body ( 201 with the stored ticket), or 202 with a run descriptor when the run waits for a person. Follow it with tuvl runs tail <run_id> or GET /api/runs/<run_id>/events (SSE). In dev mode the session key works as an admin token. 5. Change something ¶ Open specs/triage-ticket.md and add a policy. Then hand it to your coding agent (it has the tuvl-spec , tuvl-plan and tuvl-task-loop skills); tuvl referees the result: tuvl spec check # the spec is well-formed tuvl spec diff # what changed since the task list was written tuvl spec status # the tasks, with status derived from the project The agent updates specs/triage-ticket.tasks.yaml and implements the tasks (YAML engine blocks; Python only for code agents). Then run the CI gate: tuvl spec check && tuvl validate --strict && tuvl codegen --check && tuvl lock --check \ && tuvl test --strict && tuvl spec verify --strict && tuvl spec status --strict Next: the Agentic Manual and spec-driven development .
docs.title: Quickstart

docs.text: Shipping to production ¶ tuvl ship turns a project into a container image and a Helm chart. It is the same gate as CI: nothing ships that does not validate. tuvl keys generate --write # a persistent signing key (TUVL_SIGNING_KEY) tuvl ship -t registry.example.com/triage:1.0.0 --push What it does ¶ Gate. Runs the validation ( --strict also fails on warnings). A workflow with a pending agent (V010) is an error at ship time, and the project's tuvl.lock must be current. Deploy artifacts. Writes deploy/Dockerfile (pinned to the locked tuvl version), .dockerignore and a chart in deploy/chart/<name>/ . Existing files are kept unless you pass --force . Image. Runs docker build , and docker push with --push . The .dockerignore is an allowlist : only models, workflows, agents, artifacts, datasources, llms, federation, config, the lock and .tuvl/system.yaml / telemetry.yaml enter the image. Specs, task lists, tests, agent rules and skills, compose files and .env stay out; a development file in the image is refused (V027). The container runs in production mode: no dev routes, no Insight UI, JSON logs, telemetry on. Options ¶ Option Meaning -t , --tag Image reference. Defaults to <project>:<version> --no-build Write the Dockerfile and chart, skip docker build --push Push the image after a successful build --force Overwrite existing generated files --strict Treat validation warnings as errors --with-laya / --without-laya Include the Laya decision server in the chart. Default: on when an AgentModel uses provider: laya Deploy ¶ kubectl create secret generic triage-env --from-env-file=.env helm install triage deploy/chart/triage --set image.repository=registry.example.com/triage The secret must hold TUVL_SIGNING_KEY , POSTGRES_PASSWORD and the variables of every model the workflows use. A production engine refuses to start while one is missing. For separate API and worker pods: helm install triage deploy/chart/triage --set split=true --set worker.replicaCount=3 Laya in the chart ¶ When a model uses provider: laya (or with --with-laya ), the chart gains a Laya Deployment and Service, and the engine's LAYA_API_BASE points at it. laya.enabled in values.yaml switches it. model: english auto / multilingual Image docker.io/tuvl/laya-serve:<version>-en docker.io/tuvl/laya-serve:<version> Memory request / limit 2 Gi / 3 Gi 4 Gi / 5 Gi tuvl ship chooses the image and memory from your models. Set LAYA_API_KEY in the secret to require a bearer key on the server. Leave Laya out with --without-laya (or --set laya.enabled=false ) when you use a hosted model instead. Redis ¶ The chart does not include Redis. Run more than one worker ( split=true , or several replicas) and you need one: point a type: redis datasource at it with REDIS_HOST , REDIS_PORT and REDIS_PASSWORD . See Redis configuration . See also ¶ CLI reference AI Models Installation

docs.text: AI Models ¶ The AI Models section configures your AgentModel definitions — the model connections behind llm , loop and decide agents, judges and spec analysis. tuvl uses LiteLLM under the hood, which means you can connect to any major LLM provider with a single config file. File list ¶ The sidebar lists every file in your project's llms/ directory. Click any file to open the model editor. Form editor ¶ The form is split into three sections: Identity ¶ Field Description Name Snake-case identifier used to reference this model in workflow YAML (e.g. default ) Description Human-readable label shown in the portal Enabled Toggle to disable the model without deleting the file Model ¶ Field Description LLM Model string LiteLLM model identifier in provider/model-name format API Base URL Required for Ollama, LiteLLM proxy, or self-hosted deployments API Key Provider API key; use ${ENV_VAR} syntax to avoid hardcoding secrets Parameters ¶ Field Description Temperature Sampling temperature (0 = deterministic, 2 = creative). Default: 0.7 Max Tokens Maximum completion length. Leave blank to use the provider default Timeout Completion timeout in seconds. Default: 60 AgentModel YAML format ¶ kind: AgentModel version: v1 enabled: true metadata: name: default description: Local Llama 3 via Ollama spec: model: ollama/llama3 api_base: http://localhost:11434 temperature: 0.7 timeout: 60 Provider examples ¶ Ollama (local) OpenAI Anthropic LiteLLM proxy Azure OpenAI spec: model: ollama/llama3 api_base: http://localhost:11434 Run Ollama locally: ollama serve then ollama pull llama3 . spec: model: openai/gpt-4o api_key: "${OPENAI_API_KEY}" spec: model: anthropic/claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022 api_key: "${ANTHROPIC_API_KEY}" spec: model: openai/my-model api_base: http://my-litellm-proxy:4000 api_key: "${LITELLM_PROXY_KEY}" spec: model: azure/my-deployment api_base: "https://my-org.openai.azure.com" api_key: "${AZURE_OPENAI_API_KEY}" Using an AI model in a workflow ¶ Reference the model by its metadata.name in an llm or loop agent, a judge, or (for decision models) a decide agent: - id: score_cv description: Score a CV engine: llm inputs: { full_name: str, experience_years: int } outputs: { score: int } budget: { timeout: 20s, max_tokens: 800 } llm: model: default # matches AgentModel metadata.name prompt: Score this CV from 0 to 100. routes: { default: END, parse_error: END.failed, timeout: END.failed, budget_exceeded: END.failed, error: END.failed } The Decision toggle on this page creates type: decision models ( laya , jev or litellm ) for the decide engine . For a hosted decision model, set its API base and an ${ENV_VAR} API key there too. Multiple models ¶ You can define as many AgentModel files as you need. A common pattern is: llms/default.yaml — local Ollama model for fast iteration llms/production.yaml — GPT-4o or Claude for production quality llms/judge.yaml — a dedicated model for LLM-as-a-Judge test evaluation Reference them by name in each workflow step.

docs.text: API Docs ¶ The API Docs section embeds a live Swagger UI for your project's REST endpoints. Every auto-generated CRUD route, workflow execution endpoint, and auth route is visible and callable directly from the browser. What you'll find here ¶ The Swagger UI at /insight/api-docs proxies the OpenAPI schema from /docs and renders it in the portal's theme. It includes: Category Routes Workflow triggers each workflow's own trigger.http.path (e.g. POST /api/screen-candidate ), typed from its contract Runs POST /api/workflows/{name}/runs , GET /api/runs , GET /api/runs/{id} , GET /api/runs/{id}/events (SSE), GET /api/runs/{id}/export , POST /api/runs/{id}/pause\|resume\|abort\|steer Approvals GET /api/approvals , POST /api/approvals/{id} , POST /api/runs/{id}/human/{agent_id} Model CRUD /models/{model}/… — only for models that opt in with spec.api.crud Auth /auth/token , /auth/me , /auth/refresh , /auth/logout , /auth/bootstrap , /auth/oauth/{provider}/… , /auth/admin/* System /health , /registry , /admin/* , /api/artifacts MCP export ( /mcp ) isn't an OpenAPI route; see API: REST, SSE, MCP . Trying endpoints ¶ Click the Authorize button (🔒) at the top of the Swagger UI. Enter your access token in the Bearer field. Expand any endpoint, click Try it out , fill in the parameters, and click Execute . In dev mode, you can use the dev API key directly as a bearer token. Running a workflow via the API ¶ Call the workflow's own route: POST /api/screen-candidate Authorization: Bearer <token> Content-Type: application/json { "full_name": "Asha Menon", "email": "asha@example.com", "years_experience": 6, "skills": ["Python", "PyTorch", "LLMs", "RAG"] } The response is the end the run reached — its status and body : HTTP/1.1 201 Created X-Tuvl-Run-Id: 5b0d… { "id": "c9e2…", "status": "shortlisted", "fit_score": 88 } If the run waits for a person (a human agent) or outlives the request, the response is 202 with a run descriptor ( status_url , events_url , and the pending approval ). Any workflow can also be started by name with POST /api/workflows/{name}/runs . Following a run ¶ Every step is journaled. Follow a run over Server-Sent Events — the journal replays, then goes live: GET /api/runs/5b0d…/events Authorization: Bearer <token> Accept: text/event-stream id: 3 event: decision data: {"seq":3,"type":"decision","agent_id":"gate","engine":"decide","payload":{"decision":"assess","source":"rule#1"}} Reconnect with Last-Event-ID (or ?from_seq= ) to resume without gaps. Reading a run needs the runs:read scope (your own runs) or iam:admin . Event types are listed in Runtime . Raw OpenAPI schema ¶ The raw JSON schema is available at /openapi.json . Import it into Postman, Insomnia, or any API tool that accepts OpenAPI 3.x.

docs.text: Datasources ¶ The Datasources section manages your PostgreSQL connection configuration files. Each *.yaml file under datasources/ defines one named database connection. File list ¶ The sidebar lists every file in your project's datasources/ directory. Click any file to open the connection editor. The status indicator shows whether the connection was successfully established at startup: Indicator Meaning Green Connected and healthy Grey Datasource is disabled ( enabled: false ) Red Connection failed at startup Connection editor ¶ The form has two tabs: Form view — fill in host, port, database name, user, and password using familiar text inputs. tuvl shows a live YAML preview on the right as you type. YAML view — edit the raw config file directly. Useful for adding advanced connection options. Datasource YAML format ¶ kind: Datasource version: v1 enabled: true metadata: name: primary_db spec: type: postgres connection: host: "${POSTGRES_HOST:localhost}" port: "${POSTGRES_PORT:5432}" database: "${POSTGRES_DB:myapp}" user: "${POSTGRES_USER:postgres}" password: "${POSTGRES_PASSWORD:}" pool: min_size: 2 max_size: 10 Environment variable syntax ¶ tuvl connection fields support ${ENV_VAR_NAME:default_value} placeholders. At startup, tuvl substitutes the value from the environment. If the variable is not set, the default after : is used. Syntax Behaviour ${POSTGRES_HOST:localhost} Use POSTGRES_HOST env var, fallback to localhost ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD:} Use POSTGRES_PASSWORD env var, fallback to empty string ${POSTGRES_HOST} Use POSTGRES_HOST env var, no fallback (empty string if unset) Local development Set your credentials in a .env file at the project root. tuvl automatically loads .env on startup in dev mode. Multiple datasources ¶ You can define multiple datasource files for different databases (e.g. primary.yaml , analytics.yaml , test.yaml ). Each is registered by its metadata.name and can be referenced in model definitions: kind: ModelDefinition version: v1 metadata: name: AnalyticsEvent spec: datasource: analytics # references datasources/analytics.yaml table: events fields: [ ... ] If no datasource key is specified, the model uses the first enabled datasource. Automatic migrations ¶ On startup, tuvl runs CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS for every enabled model against its configured datasource. Existing tables are not dropped or truncated — only missing tables are created. For production schema migrations, use a tool like Alembic .

docs.text: Embeddings & Collections ¶ The Embeddings and Collections sections configure tuvl's vector search stack. Together they power Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) inside your workflows. Section Screenshot Embeddings Collections Concepts ¶ Embedding model — An EmbeddingModel config defines which model converts text into a vector (e.g. nomic-embed-text via Ollama, or OpenAI's text-embedding-3-small ). Collection — A VectorCollection config defines a named pgvector table: which embedding model to use, the vector dimension, and the distance metric. Think of a collection as a searchable knowledge base. Requirements ¶ Both features require: pgvector extension — installed in your PostgreSQL database: CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS vector; A connected and enabled Datasource (see Datasources ). Embeddings ¶ EmbeddingModel YAML ¶ kind: EmbeddingModel version: v1 enabled: true metadata: name: default_embeddings description: Ollama nomic-embed-text spec: model: ollama/nomic-embed-text api_base: http://localhost:11434 dimensions: 768 Field Description model LiteLLM embedding model string api_base Required for Ollama. Leave blank for cloud providers. dimensions Vector size — must match the model's output dimension Common embedding models ¶ Provider Model string Dimensions Ollama ollama/nomic-embed-text 768 Ollama ollama/mxbai-embed-large 1024 OpenAI openai/text-embedding-3-small 1536 OpenAI openai/text-embedding-3-large 3072 Cohere cohere/embed-english-v3.0 1024 Collections ¶ VectorCollection YAML ¶ kind: VectorCollection version: v1 enabled: true metadata: name: hr_knowledge_base description: HR policy documents and FAQs spec: embedding_model: default_embeddings # references EmbeddingModel metadata.name dimensions: 768 distance_metric: cosine # cosine | l2 | inner_product table: hr_documents # PostgreSQL table name Distance metrics ¶ Metric Use when cosine Most text similarity tasks (default) l2 Euclidean distance — good for dense numerical embeddings inner_product Normalised embeddings where dot product == cosine Using RAG in a workflow ¶ Search and ingest are built-in code agents with typed contracts: - id: retrieve_policy description: Find the relevant policy passages engine: code inputs: { employee_question: str } outputs: { hits: "list[json]" } # [{content, metadata, score}] code: run: tuvl.data_search with: { collection: hr_knowledge_base, query: "{{ employee_question }}", top_k: 5 } routes: { default: answer, error: END.failed } - id: ingest_policy description: Add a policy document to the knowledge base engine: code inputs: { title: str, content: str } outputs: { doc_id: uuid } code: run: tuvl.data_ingest with: { collection: hr_knowledge_base, document: "{{ content }}", metadata: { title: "{{ title }}" } } routes: { default: END, error: END.failed } Pass hits to an llm agent as an input to ground its answer. See the knowledge-base-qa example .

docs.text: Federation ¶ The Federation section configures OAuth2 / OIDC social login providers. Once configured, users can sign in with Google, GitHub, Microsoft, or any OIDC-compliant provider instead of (or in addition to) email and password. How federation works ¶ The user clicks Sign in with Google (or another provider) on the tuvl login page. tuvl redirects to the provider's OAuth2 authorisation endpoint. After the user consents, the provider redirects back to http://<your-tuvl-host>/auth/callback/<provider> . tuvl exchanges the authorisation code for an access token, fetches the user's profile, and creates or links a tuvl user account. An access token is issued and the user is logged in. Supported providers ¶ Provider Config key Google google GitHub github Microsoft (Entra) microsoft Any OIDC provider oidc Provider YAML format ¶ kind: OAuthProvider version: v1 enabled: true metadata: name: google spec: provider: google client_id: "${GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID}" client_secret: "${GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET}" scopes: - openid - email - profile For generic OIDC: kind: OAuthProvider version: v1 enabled: true metadata: name: my_sso spec: provider: oidc client_id: "${SSO_CLIENT_ID}" client_secret: "${SSO_CLIENT_SECRET}" discovery_url: "https://sso.example.com/.well-known/openid-configuration" scopes: - openid - email - profile Configuring a provider in the portal ¶ Click + New Provider to open the creation form: Field Description Provider Select from the dropdown (google, github, microsoft, oidc) Client ID OAuth2 application client ID from the provider console Client Secret Use ${ENV_VAR} syntax to reference environment variables Discovery URL Required for generic OIDC providers Scopes Space-separated list of OAuth2 scopes to request Enabled Toggle without deleting the config Callback URL ¶ Register the following redirect URI in your OAuth2 provider console: http://<your-tuvl-host>/auth/callback/<provider-name> For example, if tuvl runs at https://myapp.example.com with provider name google : https://myapp.example.com/auth/callback/google Redis required for federation in multi-worker deployments OAuth2 uses a CSRF state token that must survive until the provider's callback. In a multi-worker deployment, the callback may hit a different worker than the one that started the flow. Configure Redis to share state across workers. Role mapping ¶ By default, federated users are created with no roles. Assign roles after the first login via the IAM panel , or configure automatic role mapping based on email domain in your OAuthProvider spec: spec: provider: google client_id: "${GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID}" client_secret: "${GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET}" role_mapping: - domain: "mycompany.com" roles: ["employee"] - domain: "partner.com" roles: ["external_reviewer"]
